# A census of Arbor's tests

<!-- Generated by `scripts/census.py --write` from scripts/census-template.md. Change the words there and the judgements in the script's tables, never here. -->

Some 7,869 tests pass, and the serious faults of late were all found on a real Mac. This census asks why that can be: which
tests could **never** fail on account of what macOS really does, what each kind of test proves, how much of the code that
talks to macOS anything runs at all, and which features a person would be hurt by that nothing has yet tried on a Mac.

**Taken at commit `3b6ed59f`**, the last that changed anything it reads. Every number in sections 1 to 3 comes out of one script that reads the sources as text and builds nothing:

```bash
scripts/census.py
scripts/census.py --write
scripts/census.py --out /tmp/census
scripts/census.py --show PeekControllerTests
scripts/census.py --sample 60 --seed 4
```

The first prints the tables, the second regenerates this page whole, the third also writes one row per test (`tests.tsv`), per test file, per helper and per
file of real code. `--show` says how a test or a suite was classified and through which helpers; `--sample` draws tests at random, with their bodies, to check by hand.

**It is not part of `make check` or of CI, on purpose.** What is a judgement and not a reading stands in tables in the script, to be argued with: which members of the
stand-ins stand for the world, which suites have a tool for a subject, what a recording would have to hold for a helper to
count as seen on a Mac, what a run must switch on to get into each file of real code, which defaults the ranking in section 4 goes by. The script stops when the sources have
outgrown a table (a stand-in has a public member it has not been told about; a source line its reading of the wiring rests on is gone; a default has changed), or when a recording holds what the page says none does. Then a person looks. So
the page is as old as the commit above: take it again after a change to the stand-ins, to the real-window runs or to what ships switched on.

## The answer in short

- **7,599 of 7,863 test functions (96.6 %) cannot fail because of anything macOS does**: they never meet it. 2,382 are
  arithmetic, 404 try the test tools themselves, 4,813 run the real controller against stand-ins.
- Of those 4,813, **3,777 have the world act, and the world is the fake**. 1,111 of them (29 %) rest on at least one
  report or answer that no committed recording of a Mac holds; 1,738 on one that is either unrecorded or known to differ
  from the recording; 2,039 only on what a recording bears out.
- **3 test functions replay real behaviour**, in 193 cases: 95 recordings of a real Mac, 92 of them held to what Arbor did on
  the way and not only to where it ended, by 1,784 lines of expectation. Somebody has seen 6 of them fail; 0 lines name a fault that is
  not cured here. (At the last census: 2 functions, 39 recordings, none held to what Arbor did on the way.) All are from one kind of hosted Mac and
  one version of macOS, 1024×768 or 1600×900, all but a few with one display. They now hold windows opening, switches between apps, shortcuts pressed, full
  screen and the Space it makes, an app that hangs, the wallpaper's sweep, and, from the first run that recorded itself, an app coming forward, a native tab and a key held for a peek. Since the night of this census: a display that comes, and Spaces of the person's own, changed with real keys.
  No recording holds a display going, text being typed, or the permission being taken away.
- **86 functions run real macOS code**, 61 of them drawing into bitmaps in memory. None calls the Accessibility API, receives
  or posts an event, registers a shortcut or puts a window on the screen.
- Of the 7,886 lines that only a Mac can run, **at least 1,227 lines and 133 branches are run by nothing automatic**: no
  test, and neither of the two real-window runs CI makes. That includes 6 % of the input layer: the event taps, the shortcuts, the
  pinch, the rectangle. Another 3,875 lines are in files that an automatic run enters only in part.
- **What could hurt a person most is what is checked least** (section 4): the shortcuts, which are on from the first launch, and the event taps, which hold every event of the Mac once somebody
  switches the gestures on, are switched off in both automatic runs.

## 1. What each test touches

Each `@Test` function is put into exactly one class by what its body touches, and the helpers it calls in its own test target,
followed by name up to five calls deep (a file's `makeHarness()`, a `Desk` with an `init`, a suite kept in a property, an
extension of `Harness`).

| Class | What it is | What it proves | What it takes on trust |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** pure | Values in, values out: trees, layout, geometry, parsing, settings, state machines | The arithmetic is right | That the question is the right one. macOS cannot make it fail, and need not |
| **B** a stand-in or a tool | The subject is the fake, the harness, the chaos lab, the trace recorder and replayer, benchmarks, or the repository's own text read as text | The instruments work | Nothing about Arbor on a Mac |
| **C** commands only | The real controller on stand-ins. Windows are opened; everything else is a command, a shortcut pressed and let go, or time passing | Given this arrangement, this command gives that tree, view, reply, overlay | That `setFrame` and `focus` do as told and are echoed as the fake echoes them |
| **D** the world acts | As C, and the test has macOS, an app or a hand do something, or tells the stand-in what macOS or an app will answer | **If** macOS reports this, in this order, Arbor copes | The *if*: the order and content of reports the fake makes up |
| **E** a recording | A trace from `collab/evidence/traces` is replayed against the controller | Today's Arbor copes with what that Mac reported and those apps answered on that day, and moves each window as often, and after the same reports, as the trace's `.expect` file says | That the layer below the seam would still make the same events of it |
| **F** real macOS code | Compiled only on macOS, calling AppKit, Carbon, CoreGraphics or Arbor's macOS-only types | That piece of real code does what the test looks at | - |
| **G** real files, sockets, processes, queues | POSIX and Dispatch for real, the same on macOS and Linux | The control socket, the state and settings files, the log, the lock, the scheduler | - |

Where a test touches several, the order of precedence is F, E, B, G, D, C, A.

**How they were counted.** The sources hold 7,869 `@Test` attributes. 6 stand in the `#else` of an `#if os(macOS)` or
`#if canImport(…)` as `@Test(.disabled(…)) func sameName() {}`, so that Linux reports the test as skipped: the same function
written twice, counted once. That leaves 7,863. A parameterised test (`@Test(arguments:)`, 805 of them) is one function
however many cases it runs. 89 functions are compiled only on macOS: the 86 of class F, and 3 that hand the Mac shell's helper tools to
the compiler (class B; a change in Apple's SDK could fail those). 5 carry `.enabled(if:)`; 0 are disabled on the platform they are written for. 7 wrap
a finding in `withKnownIssue`: the chaos lab's random walks, which report a script nobody knows and do not fail on it, and in `PromisesTests` the promises the trunk breaks, each with its row on the board.

**Reading it.**

- **A, 30 %.** The whole of `ArborCoreTests` but 21 functions. It is the firmest ground there is and it says nothing about a Mac.
  Within class A: 367 functions in 14 files try the pure types that `ArborKit/AX` and `ArborKit/Input` go by and the controller hardly knows (named in at most two of its files): `AppThatCameForward`, `AppsDoubleClick`, `DesktopGuardZones`, `EchoFilter`, `FramePlan`, `GestureInterpreter`, `GestureRouter`, `GestureUpdate`, `InputActivity`, `MacTiling`, `NativeTabs`, `PointerSurface`, `RectangleGesture`, `RetrySchedule`, `ScrollClaim`, `StackedWindow`, `StrayDialog`, `SweptAside`, `SystemShortcuts`, `TapHealth`, `WindowGrab`, `WindowKind`. They are arithmetic, and what they are fed is a sequence of reports that the test made up.
  So the decisions of the two layers nearest to macOS are well tried *as decisions*; whether macOS sends what they are fed is
  the same open question as in class D, one level down.
- **C, 13 %.** The world holds still. 211 of them let time pass; 124 open a window after the start, which by the definition used here is
  set-up, though it is a report like any other (table 2 counts it). Every one of them also meets the fake's echoes, which
  `Harness.run` delivers after each command.
- **D, 48 %.** The largest class. In 3,304 the fake (or the test itself, calling the controller's event methods) sends a report or a hand works one of
  Arbor's panels; in 466 the test only tells a stand-in what to answer (a minimum size, where the pointer is, what the Mac's facts are); 7 are
  random walks of the chaos lab. 1,044 are in D only through a helper: a `makeHarness()` that ends with `userFocus`, say.
- **E, 3 functions, 193 cases.** Two run once per trace, 96 cases each. One replays the trace and holds its end, and now its course, to the
  `.expect` file beside it. The other cuts every trace wherever something may have changed, in over two thousand places, and tries every way back
  to a Mac with all its windows in sight. The third is a control: it takes out of `app-switch-unreported` the one report that was lost on the Mac, and asks that
  the expectations fail. It is the one headless kind that holds real behaviour, and it holds it as a fossil: it fails
  when Arbor changes, never when macOS does.
- **F, 1 %.** See table 1a. **G, 2 %** is real and is the same on both platforms; nothing in it is about windows.

what macOS says of itself (the keyboard layouts, its own shortcuts). The others draw. Functions that name anything of the Accessibility API: 0.

### How far the classifier can be trusted

It reads text. It does not know types, so it follows names: a bare call to a member of the enclosing suite, then to the file,
then to the target; `.name` to the test target's types that have been named so far, and to its extensions of other
people's types; overloads by their argument labels. What a helper does is held against every test that reaches it,
whether or not that branch of the helper runs.

Checked by hand at commit `a391fe4`, each test read with its helpers, against the definitions above:

| Round | Drawn | Read | Wrong class | What was wrong, and what became of it |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | seed 1, eight from each class | 50 | 1 | A restart after a crash counted as the world acting (`restartedAfterAccident`). It is Arbor's own life: taken off the list, with what the memory store is told it found |
| 2 | seed 2, from all | 60 | 1 | A test that only compares paths counted as real files. Class G now wants a file read, written, made or removed |
| 3 | seed 3, from all | 60 | 0 | |
| 4 | seed 4, from all | 60 | 0 | One right class for a wrong reason (`controller.shortcut(for:)`, a question, taken for a key going down): mended |

**Two wrong in 230 (0.9 %). None in the last 120**, whose classes are the same under the final rules as when they were read; by the rule of
three that puts the error rate below 2.5 % with 95 % confidence. A seed draws other tests once a test has been added or removed, so the rounds can be
drawn again only at that commit.

Random samples were not what found the large mistakes. Reading the table per file, and three sweeps aimed at the classifier's weak
spots (calls in classes A and C that resolve to nothing known; helpers that have the world act and are not reached; tests in D only through a
helper), found these, all mended before round 3: 92 pure tests taken for D because a pure function has a `minimumSize:` label too; some
70 taken for G because private types of the same name in different files were merged; a dozen whose helper lives in another suite kept in a
property; seven where a loop that copies the windows of one run of Arbor into the next was taken for windows closing; four
`scenariosCan…` tests whose subject is the `expect` language; chaos scripts written on one line. `scripts/census.py --self-test` holds the script to most of these on small sources.

**Soft spots that remain.** Whether a suite's subject is a tool is a judgement (the list is in the script; 302 functions hang on
it). "Answers only" is the softest edge of D: a `makeHarness()` that puts the pointer somewhere makes the tests about the look of tiles class D. Budget
tests that go through `BenchmarkCase` are in B as benchmarks, though what they pin is the controller's thrift. A test that gets a saved
state out of a harness and then only decodes it is C.

## 2. Class D: what the fake is trusted with

For each helper that stands for the world: how many tests rest on it, and whether what it reports has ever been held against a recording of a real
Mac. The evidence looked for:

- **Recordings**: `collab/evidence/traces/*.jsonl`. For each helper the script names the kind of line a recording would have to hold
  (`setFullScreen`: a `changed` whose window says `fullScreen`; `setDisplays`: a `displaysChanged` after which a display has come, gone, moved or
  changed size, not merely lost two points to the Dock; `revokeAccessibility`: the answer no to `mayUseAccessibility`, not merely the question) and lists
  the traces from a Mac that hold one.
- **Known differences**: the table "What real macOS does that `FakeWindowSystem` does not" in the traces' README, for the rows where the fake, read today,
  still does otherwise; and what the recordings made since show and that table does not have yet, with the trace that shows it.
- **Citations**: comments in `Sources/ArborTesting` and `FaithfulFakeTests`, which pins the fake's order of reports. Both cite
  `collab/evidence/ax-events.txt`. **That file is not in the repository**, so what they cite cannot be checked from here.
- **Outcomes on real windows**: whether `arbor-e2e` or `e2e-drag.sh`, which CI runs on a Mac, bring the same situation about. They check where windows end up,
  not what macOS reported on the way: a sign that Arbor copes, no check of the fake.
- **Real input once**: `collab/evidence/gestures-latest.txt`, one run of `proof.sh` (table 2d).

"report": the fake, or the test itself, sends Arbor an event. "answer": the test tells a stand-in what to say when asked. "panel": a hand on one of Arbor's own
panels, played by calling the action the real panel would call.

Of the 3777 tests of class D, 1111 rest on at least one premise that no committed recording covers, and 1738 on at least one that is either uncovered or known to differ from the recording. 2039 rest only on premises a recording bears out.

A premise of another kind, which no longer holds: `open` gave every window process 1000 unless told otherwise. 2263 of the 4266 tests of classes C and D that open windows never name a process, so all their apps were one process; 180 of those close or minimize a window, after which the fake hands the keyboard to "the app's next window", which there was any window at all. Now every app name is a process of its own (`FakeWindowSystem.process(of:)`). Three tests fell when it became so.

### What the recordings hold

| The recordings as tests |  |
|---|---:|
| Recordings from a real Mac that a test replays | 95 |
| Test functions that replay a recording (class E) | 3 |
| Test cases: a function that takes the traces as arguments runs once for each | 193 |
| Recordings whose `.expect` file holds Arbor to what it did on the way (`moved …`) | 92 |
| Lines of expectation in the `.expect` files of the recordings | 1784 |
| Recordings whose test somebody has seen fail: by the README's last column, or by a control among the tests | 6 |
| Known problems: `problem` lines, each a fault the recording shows and nobody has cured here | 0 |

When this census was last taken, at commit `a8180c5`, it was 2 functions, 80 cases and 39 recordings, with 54 lines of expectation, all of them about the end: no recording was held to what
Arbor did on the way, and nowhere was it written down who had seen a test fail. Two things have changed what a recording costs: every run on a hosted Mac is recorded without anybody thinking of it, and
`scripts/trace-to-test.py` makes a test of a trace in one command (`docs/TRACES.md`). It also writes the `.expect` file: how often Arbor moved each window and after which line of the trace, where each ended up, whom Arbor asked to take the keyboard.
**A test that nobody has seen fail only holds today's behaviour in place**, and that is 89 of the 95: what they would catch is not known. (The README also tells of older traces that went red
when B1, B3, B5, B6 and B7, the bugs they showed, were cured. It keeps no column for them, and they are not counted.)

96 traces, 95 of them from a Mac. Systems: macOS Version 26.6.2 (Build 25G83) (95), simulated (1). Builds of Arbor that recorded on the Mac: dev (60), dev (a51104d) (35). Displays there: 1024×768 (70), 1600×900 (23), 1920×1080 + 1280×800 (2). Days: 2026-10-14 (60), 2026-10-15 (35). Apps whose windows are in them, and in how many: ArborTestWindows (54), TextEdit (29), Finder (28), Terminal (25), Safari (23), System Settings (23), Calendar (19), Notes (19), Preview (19), Mail (18), Calculator (5).

Reports of `WindowSystemEvents` (and `shortcut`) that occur in no recording from a Mac: `accessibilityWasRefused`, `dragCancelled`, `doubleClickReached`.

53 of the 95 recordings have lines of the kind the format calls "recorded by name" for the questions Arbor has learnt to ask since the first were made: `mayUseAccessibility` in 52, `stackedWindows` in 23,
`inputActivity` in 15, `modifierKeysDown` in 9, `windowsFrontToBack` in 4, `isHolding` in 3. **A question that was asked is not yet the answer a test makes up.** `mayUseAccessibility` was always answered yes, `modifierKeysDown` with no key
but in 1 (`space-window-carried`: ⌃ held with a window in the hand), `windowsFrontToBack` never with an empty list, `isHolding` in the course of a tap and, once, of a peek. So the script asks for the answer, and no recording holds the others. `macTiling` is in 5: with every switch on, as a Mac comes, in two; with those for the screen's edges and the menu bar off, as a script had set them, in three. `secondsSinceClickOrModifierKey` and `strayDialogsWaiting`
are in no recording even as questions.

**Reading it.**

- **`userFocus` carries 1,583 of the 3,777 tests of class D.** 20 recordings hold a focus report after a press, and 23 now hold a switch from one app to another, which the
  helper stands for as well: by an icon in the Dock, by ⌘Tab, by a click into a window. As a rule the Mac sent one `focused` with a `keyboardFocusMoved` before and after it, and now and then no `focused` at all. The fake announces
  the app and then the window, once each, and then says twice that the keyboard has moved: the order most often recorded where nobody pressed anything. Its word about the app, `applicationActivated`, is in 2 recordings, all from the first run after the mend: the builds before handed it to the controller past the recorder. In `two-apps-by-clicks` a switch arrives as the press, `keyboardFocusMoved`, the app 60 ms after the press, the window, and `keyboardFocusMoved` again.
- **A window opening is in 5 recordings now**, 9 windows in all: ⌘N in an app that runs, with everything in view and while framed; an app opened again after it quit; an app started from the Dock. 537 tests of class D (713 of all classes) open one
  while Arbor runs. The order the fake uses (appeared, then focused) is what all but one of them show, 6 ms to half a second apart; the first window of the app that was started was followed by no `focused`. `FaithfulFakeTests` still pins that order to a file that is not here.
- **Displays were the largest premise with nothing behind it at all, and have a beginning**: 459 tests on `setDisplays` and 54 on a silent change of the list. 3 recordings hold a
  display that comes (`display-plugged-in`, `-again`, `display-retina-plugged-in`: a virtual one, which `check-displays.sh` plugs in when somebody starts it) and 2 begin with two. No recording holds one that goes, moves or changes its size by itself, so the tests on `setDisplays`, which does all of it, still count as resting on nothing recorded; and there is no
  real-window run in CI. What the other recordings have under `displaysChanged` is the Dock growing by two points.
- **Keys.** 10 recordings hold the key of a shortcut going down and coming up as two reports (57 lines), which is what `keyDown` and `keyUp` make up (107 and 100 tests). In the days every ⌃⌥Space was up again within a quarter of
  a second; 1 recording, `peek-with-a-real-key`, holds one held for a second, which is a peek. No recording holds a key that repeats. A modifier held during a drag (26 and 15) is in 1, `space-window-carried`: ⌃, for a change of Space with a window in the hand. No automatic run has shortcuts switched on.
- **Typing** (58). What Arbor asks is `inputActivity`, and in 4 recordings the count of keys rises from one answer to the next. The keys were shortcuts. Nobody typed into a window; at the seam that looks the same.
- **Spaces** (81). The only Space in a recording is the one full screen makes (12 recordings): every other window is reported off the Space, and not as anybody's move, which is how the fake does it. A second Desktop of the person's own is in none. `windowFound`, which `setListed` (35)
  makes up for a window on a Space that was not showing, is only in `hang-start`, for the windows of an app that hung while Arbor started.
- **The permission** (115, 68, 50). The question is in 52 recordings, which bears out `watchAccessibility` (179) and no more: no recording holds it being taken away.
- **Full screen** (81) is in 8 recordings, Safari and TextEdit, by the green button and by ⌃⌘F, and went straight into table 2b. Each of them showed a fault, the window seen at its old frame before Arbor put it in its slot, was written down as a known problem while the cure was a branch, and said so by itself when the cure landed: they hold it in place now, and fail without it.
- **An app that hangs** (66) is in 3 recordings: a `setFrame` on its window comes back after a second with nothing.
- **An app that comes forward** by itself (47). `app-switch-unreported` is a recording of just that, and what it shows is that the report the fake makes up did not come: its `focused` line was added by hand, for what `AXWindowSystem` reports since it was cured.
  What tells Arbor that nobody touched anything, `secondsSinceClickOrModifierKey`, has no recorded answer.
- **The wallpaper's sweep** (7, 2, 1). 3 recordings hold what the fake makes up: the window server lists the windows at the sides of the display while their apps have them where they were. A trace cannot tell a press on a strip from one on the wallpaper; the remarks in those recordings do. In a third, `day-10-click-on-the-wallpaper`, Arbor had no reason to ask the window server, and all it heard was the press and that the keyboard had moved: of no window that it had.
- **macOS's own tiling.** What it does to a window that is let go at the side of the display is in 2 recordings. Which of its switches are on, which Arbor asks when a drag begins and 106 tests tell the fake (`tiling`), is answered in 5 recordings: all of them on, which is macOS's default, in two; those for the screen's edges and the menu bar off, as a script had set them, in three.
- **Native tabs** (34) are in 3 recordings, of `arbor-e2e`'s three steps about them: a tab opens in a docked window, the first is chosen again, the one in front closes. On test windows; no stock app's tabs yet. In the one run of `proof.sh` on record,
  full screen came out 3 ✔ 4 ✘ and the app coming forward 4 ✔ 1 ✘.
- Where there *is* a recording it has earned its keep: the helpers of table 2b are known to differ because somebody could look. Drags are the plainest case: 186 tests use a `drag`
  that begins before the window moves, and the 19 recordings that hold one show a drag that begins a fifth to a third of a second late, on a window that has already moved and, if it did not have the keyboard, has been focused first (which the fake now plays: `press`). In `day-11-drags-to-the-edges` a drag is never reported as one at all.
- The recordings are one kind of Mac on 2 days. A premise marked "recorded" has been seen a few times at most, on test windows or 10 stock apps, on macOS 26.6.2, on one display of 1024×768 or 1600×900.

## 3. The other side: real code and who runs it

Every file that only a Mac can run or that stands at the edge: lines of code (not blank, not only a comment), branches (`if`, `guard`, `while`, each `case` and `default` of a `switch`; not
`??`, `?:` or `catch`), and what executes it.

**Automatic** means: CI does it without being asked, as `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `linux.yml` stand. That is every test on Linux (in parts, and a last job sees that none was lost: `scripts/fast-tests.py`); on a Mac the tests a Mac can say something about (`scripts/ci-tests.py`: whatever stands behind a compile-time condition, so all of class F, and
real files, sockets and processes, so class G; every test once a night); the smoke scripts on both; and two steps of the one macOS job, `arbor-e2e --full-screen` and `scripts/mac-shell/e2e-drag.sh`, whose verdict the job `real-windows` passes on. The macOS job is left out when `scripts/ci-changes.py` finds that a Mac could prove nothing new. **By hand** means a Mac shell script
that runs only when somebody starts it (`workflow_dispatch`).

**How it was read.** There is no coverage measurement, so this is a reading of the wiring. Both automatic runs start the real app with `ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=1`, `ARBOR_NO_STATUS_ITEM=1`,
`ARBOR_NO_PROMPT=1` and `ARBOR_ONLY_PIDS=…`, on hosted Macs that come with Reduce Motion on. For each file the script holds what a run must switch on or send to get into it at all, and asks
each run and each script whether it does. A file that an automatic run gets into counts as run **whole**. For class F the names a test reaches are followed on into the sources, member by member, and whatever is reached
counts whole as well. Both are generous, so **the lines nothing runs are a lower bound**.

What each automatic run brings. **e2e**: tile, watchdog; commands sent: activate, arrange, back, desktop, dock, exclude, find, float, float-all, get, include, layout, pause, quit, relayout, reload-settings, resize, resume, reveal, set, settings-window, show-all, show-shortcuts, state, status, toggle-auto-dock, trace, zoom. **e2e-drag**: ctl, drag, hotkeys; commands sent: dock, float, show-all. (watchdog: left on; tile: a window refuses its slot; drag: the real pointer drags; ctl: `arborctl` is used.)

The macOS-only part of the product (ArborKit/AX, ArborKit/UI, ArborKit/Input, ArborKit/App): 7886 lines, 873 branches; nothing runs 1227 lines (16 %) and 133 branches of it automatically, and 3875 more lines are in files an automatic run enters only in part.

**Reading it.**

- **The input layer is dark.** 62 of its 1,087 lines and 13 of its 134 branches run only when somebody starts a script: `HotKeyCenter`, `GestureTap`, `RectangleFramer`, `PointerInput`, `DesktopProbe`, `WindowList`, and in
  `EventTap` everything from installing a tap to its callback. One switch does it: both automatic runs set `ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=1`. These are the callbacks macOS holds every event of the system for.
  Their decisions are among the best tried code there is (367 pure tests); that an event ever reaches them is checked by `input-taps.sh`, by hand.
- **What a person touches first is dark too**: the menu bar item (191 lines), the welcome window's own half (192), the name field (119), the minimap's panel (106), the stage that plays every motion (199, because
  the hosted Macs reduce motion), the update window (32).
- **`CallSensor` (117 lines) is run by nothing whatever**: not under `ARBOR_ONLY_PIDS`, and no script switches its settings on. They ship off.
- **"Automatic, in part" is where the weight is.** `AXWindowSystem.swift`, 1,131 lines and 222 branches, 25 % of all the branches in the macOS-only code, is entered by both runs, with a handful of test windows of one obliging app (and a second app for a
  moment) on one display. Whatever only other apps, a second display, Spaces or a slow Mac bring about in it is not entered, and nothing says how much that is. `compat.sh` puts thirteen stock apps in front of it, by hand.
- **Entered is not looked at.** The runs compare frames with the window server's and see that some panels are there. Nothing automatic clicks a tile, drags a gap handle, types into Go to… or the settings window, or looks at the hint that shows after the first real dock.
- **The edge that is well covered** is the one that is not macOS: the control socket (32 and 28 tests of class G, both real-window runs, two smoke scripts).

## 4. Features and what has been seen of them on a Mac

Sections 1 to 3 count tests and lines. This one asks the same of features: which have no check on real windows at all, which have one that nobody runs automatically, which have one that has never
run; **ranked by how much a person would be hurt if the feature misbehaved on a real Mac**. It is a reading by a person, not a count: the words are in the template, and the script only
holds it to the facts it goes by: the defaults in `Settings.swift`, which commands have a default shortcut, that every script named exists, and that what stands between quotation marks is still said by a spec, a step or a comment.

**The measure**, in this order:

1. **What the worst fault does.** **1**: input blocked for the whole Mac; a window lost, hidden or stuck; something moved that nobody moved. **2**: a jolt, the wrong window, a wrong view, keys that go to the wrong place. **3**: cosmetic.
2. **Is it within reach as Arbor ships?** *always* (it works from the first launch without being asked) and *key* (on a default shortcut) count alike; then *menu*: an item of the menu; *asked for*: only by a setting, a shortcut of one's own or `arborctl`; *off*: ships switched off.
3. **Has its macOS half ever run on a Mac?** *never*, by the spec's own words; *not said*; *in part* (an earlier state, other keys, by command and not by hand); *yes*.
4. **Does CI run a check of it?** *no*; *in part* (by command, where a person uses a key or the pointer; or a step that cannot fail); *yes*.

Ties go first to what is known to fail today, then to what is met more often. **Where the facts are from**: each spec's status line and Shipped note in `docs/features/`, read at commit `a8180c5`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; and the runs made on hosted Macs on 2026-10-14 and 15 (macOS 26.6.2, one 1024×768 display), whose
outputs are not committed: given as passed/failed. Several specs still say that their macOS half has not been compiled: since CI builds everything on a hosted Mac, that much is out of date for all of them, and *never* below means never run.

**The order is that of 2026-10-14 and is kept**, so that "rank 1, 2 or 3" in `collab/QUESTIONS.md` (Q26) goes on meaning the same rows. The columns are kept current, since they decide defaults: by the measure above, ranks 1 and 2 would stand lower today.

**It was read whole when the census was first taken, and not since.** What the recordings have changed was read again at the commit above: ranks 4, 5, 10 and 25. The column "Ever run?", the checks to make next, the lists below the table and the fifth conclusion were
brought up to the runs of the night and morning of 2026-10-15 for ranks 1 to 5, 7, 8, 12, 13, 16 to 22 and 26, from the runs' own outputs. Since then Arbor ships nine shortcuts (`shortcuts` "core") where it shipped some fifty: "As it ships" says so for ranks 16, 17, 20 and 24, whose keys are among those that went. Otherwise the columns "Worst fault" and "As it ships" of the ranks not named here are as old as the census, and Arbor ships with less switched on by now than they say.

In the first all sixteen follow one early step: launched without the permission and then granted by the script's way (the privacy database written, its daemon restarted), Arbor did not start by itself within twelve seconds. `input-taps.sh`, session 4, passed: the permission reset for everybody, Arbor's taps are gone within three seconds and it says so; input afterwards could not be tried, the script's own tools having lost the permission too. **A probe that takes it from Arbor alone**, with a stream of presses, keys and notches to a witness, in rounds with and without Arbor and with and without its taps: with taps installed, events are lost from the moment macOS withdraws the permission until Arbor has taken its taps out; none is lost without Arbor, or with Arbor and no tap. That is why no tap ships. The sixteen are explained too: a process that runs learns of a grant only through a notification, which writing to the database does not send: the script's fault. **Mended, it ran again the same night: 30/1**, the one its own again (it took the window that asks for the permission back for something left over): the loss noticed in 0.6 s with windows out of view, the taps gone, four ways home registered, the warning sign and the window up; given back, every window in view, the taps and all shortcuts back, Back returns to the view. Mended once more: 32/0 | Why a grant took Arbor seven to nine seconds to hear of in that run, and one loss nearly seven (criterion 10 says three): the script's haste with the daemon, or Arbor. ### No real-window check exists at all

- **Built, and within reach**: F11 (no rule has ever placed a real window), F25 (a display's name and kind come from macOS and have not been seen), F33 (but for `gapHandles`), F35 (places kept for windows on other Spaces: built, though its
  status line says "ready"; its criterion 6 is a script still to write), F57 on test windows (rank 6).
- **Built, and needs none**: F62 ("Nothing here is macOS-only"). F50's shipped parts and F28's replays are headless by nature; every Mac shell script uses `arborctl`, and `trace-demo.sh` records.
- **Not built**: F04, F14, F34, F52, F59.

### A check exists and has never run, by the spec's own words

On 2026-10-14 there were fourteen: F08, F13, F20, F22, F26, F41, F44 (with real keys), F49, F51, F53, F55, F58, F60 (the guard), F63; and `shots-finder.sh`, the half of F27 that presses keys.

**By noon of 2026-10-15 the script of every one of the fourteen had been played on a hosted Mac to its last line, once or more.** That is all the sentence says. It does not say green: F51, F22, F26, F44, F63 and F20 have had a run without a failure, F63 at the third and F20 at the second; every step about F55 passed, in a script whose failures are the guard's; F08, F13, F41, F58 and `shots-finder.sh` ended their last run with failures that are their scripts' own, but for the palette's two (rank 21); F49 and F53 are red by a fault that is known (rank 12); the guard is red and shelved. It does not say today's code: each of those runs played the plain branch of its hour. **At noon twelve of the scripts were played on one commit of the trunk** (`4ff9daa9`, three Macs): 846 passed, 29 failed. `check-F51.sh`, `check-displays.sh`, `check-F63.sh`, `check-F20.sh`, `shots-minimap.sh`, `check-F44.sh` and `shots-F22.sh` without a failure. Of the 29, seven were the scripts' own or a tool's, thirteen the shelved guard's with three more in their wake, and six Arbor's, each on the board already (1.63 once, 1.64 four times, 4.19 once): none was new. F49, F53 and F13 were not among the twelve, and the trunk has since come to ship nine shortcuts, which that commit did not. And it does not say a hand, a real keyboard, a real app, a cable or a lid: every key, click and scroll was posted by a script. **Never run at all**: `watchdog-bundle.sh` (F13) and `desktop-facts.sh` (F60). The real-window suite ran on hosted Macs on 2026-10-14 and has seen three more features at work without running their scripts: a window kept in view (F49: red, a kept window of another app stays behind the key window), summon (F53), pause by its key (F40); and in part F41 and the default shortcuts of F22, each of which it pressed once (143/0).

### Ships off until seen

`guardDesktopClicks` (F60), `continuousZoom` (F16), `windowPictures` (F02), `minimapDuration` 0 (F26), `holdStillWhileCameraIsOn` and `holdStillWhileMicrophoneIsOn` (F58), `soleFloatTakesDesktop` (F18), `newWindows` "float" (F23),
`reflowWhileDragging` (F09), `tabsEnabled` (F04), `automaticUpdateChecks` (F13). That is the right default for what nobody has seen. The same rule had not been applied to `peek`, `scrollZoom` and the ⌃⌥ rectangle. Since 2026-10-15 it is (Q26): `peek` passed its check and
stays on; everything that needs an event tap is off behind one switch, `pointerGestures`.

## What the numbers suggest

1. **The suite proves "if macOS says this, Arbor copes", 3,777 times, and checks the *if* in 95 recordings.** Faults found on a Mac are what that shape predicts. More tests of class D add nothing on that side. Recordings do: with 39 of them, 1,220 of 2,361 tests of
   class D (52 %) rested on something no recording holds; with 95 it is 1,111 of 3,777 (29 %).
2. **A recording is the cheapest thing that turns a premise into a fact**, and it stays a test. Since the last census that has been done for a window opening, a switch between apps by ⌘Tab, by the Dock and by click, a shortcut pressed, full screen, a hang and the wallpaper's sweep, and it takes one command
   now (`trace-to-test.py`). The first run that recorded itself added an app coming forward, a key held for a peek, native tabs and macOS's answer about its own tiling. By table 2a the next to make: a second display plugged in and out, the permission taken away, a modifier held during a drag, a Space of the person's own, a hand on Go to…. The scripts exist (`check-displays.sh`, `check-F63.sh`, `check-F09.sh`, `check-desktop.sh`, `shots-finder.sh`), and each
   leaves its traces behind. And **each new test should be seen to fail once** (`trace-to-test.py --cure`): 89 of 95 have not been.
3. **`collab/evidence/ax-events.txt` should be in the repository or stop being cited.** `FaithfulFakeTests` holds the fake to it.
4. **One more automatic session with the switches off** (`ARBOR_NO_HOTKEYS=0`, `ARBOR_NO_STATUS_ITEM=0`, Reduce Motion off) on the hosted Mac, with a few real keys, one pinch, one ⌃⌥-drag and one click in the menu bar, would bring most of the 1,227 lines under an automatic run, and the first two ranks of table 4 with them. The scripts exist.
5. **Fourteen features had a check that was written and had never run; none is left.** Running each once on a hosted Mac is the largest gain for the least work on this page. The first evening bore that out: of the five scripts that ran, two passed, and the three that failed cost a default (no event tap ships), found a drag that is never seen, and shelved a feature. The night bore out something else: **a count of greens is not a reading.** Most failures were the scripts' own, or followed from one fault that was on the board already (rank 12, the raise); what was new and Arbor's lay mostly behind greens: a minimized window fetched back during a hold, windows out of view in plain view while displays change, the keyboard taken from an app Arbor does not look at, one shrink in six moves. Each was found by reading the trace of a run that had passed. And a question the scripts could not answer (does the keyboard go back after a panel?) was settled in a minute and a half by a script written for it, with a control before every claim. What none of this gives yet is one commit on which all fourteen have been played: twelve have been, once. That is asked of the candidate for the next build, at the switches that ship: each script green, or each failure with its verdict written down beforehand.
6. **Measure instead of reading.** Table 3 is an argument from the wiring. The macOS job could build Arbor with coverage instrumentation and publish what the two runs really execute; `AXWindowSystem.swift` is where that would tell most.
